rv.q: More than a little fun, as it turns out, as Giulia is a grand, gothic, and often incoherent but deeply felt passion project from someone new to the world of writing musical theater who, in her first outing in the form, has thrown together a brew of every trope that interests her at once.

Nettles's occasionally stirring, tonally muddled telling — which opened on Friday at the Arts Center in a deluxe production directed by Mary Zimmerman — Giulia is a brave champion of feminist sisterhood, delivering rote empowerment through musical numbers.
With Zimmerman’s expert direction, Giulia: The Poison Queen of Palermo has that magical stage chemistry that fuses disparate elements into a work of undeniable beauty.
This world première production of Giulia: The Poison Queen of Palermo is presented by the Arts Center (PAC NYC). It is a remarkable and resonant theatrical experience.
Not yet perfect but pleasurable, often artfully done and a lot of fun, the musical is written and composed by Jennifer Nettles, who delivers an exuberant performance as the heroic Giulia.
There is much to love, and much to cheer for, in Giulia: The Poison Queen of Palermo, down to its fantastic “encore” song.
Gorgeous sets, eye-catching costuming, and a strong cast singing catchy songs make Giulia the queen of the hour, even if the bite of its poison doesn't quite deliver.

Jennifer Nettles’ lavishly produced new musical at the Arts Center is a curious contradiction: a feast for the eyes and forcefully performed, but hampered by blunt characterizations, an uneven score and an earnest tone that makes the evening heavier than it ought to be.
Giulia sometimes gives the sense of trying very hard to be something that it is not—Hamilton, for example—while not yet embracing the pleasurably rageful id at its core.
Right now, Giulia is an intriguing cocktail, but it could stand to be a little pickier about what goes into the potion.
Giulia lays out several promising ingredients which director Mary Zimmerman doesn’t properly batch into a satisfying elixir, failing mainly as a cohesive narrative about Tofana’s life.
There are kernels of good songs in Nettles’ score, but every catchy tune gets swamped by Cian McCarthy’s orchestrations that bring a “Les Miz”-overstatement to each of them.
Together, these artists have masterfully crafted a richly theatrical musical. A Broadway transfer would come as little surprise—and would certainly feel well deserved.

Date: July 10, 2026. Author: Thom Geier Jennifer Nettles, the Grammy-winning singer-songwriter best known for her work with the alt-country duo Sugarland, is a one-woman force of nature. She not only wrote the score and book for the messy but memorable musical Giulia: The Poison Queen of Palermo but ...

cn.t: Critics find this visually stunning musical about a 17th-century poisoner compelling but uneven, praising Nettles' ambitious quadruple-threat work and the production's artistry while noting the tone skews too earnest for its darkly entertaining subject matter.

vr.q: I can't say that this is the tidiest or most thoughtfully rendered story, but actually my biggest gripe with the show was the lyrics more than the book or the music.
